newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe bourse expensive but set for robust 1997.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe bourse expensive but set for robust 1997.

text.p: The Zimbabwe Stock Exchange is likely to enjoy a robust performance in 1997 but shares remain expensive because of a lack of market liquidity, the exchange's chief executive Anthony Barfoot told Reuters.
"The chances are that, although prices are high and a correction somewhere can't be ruled out, it looks like 1997 could be another good year," he said.
But the average price/earnings ratio of 20 was very high and could discourage investors. "They will be more cautious," Barfoot said.
Neighbouring South Africa's average p/e ratio is an estimated 18, Nigeria's 12.5 and Ghana's eight.

"The main problem on the exchange is a lack of liquidity. The (exchange) is expensive. The p/e is very high because the local population are trying to buy shares and if you want a share, you will pay (a great deal) for it," Barfoot said.
Zimbabwe needs more new listings. In addition to certain pending listings there was a lot of discussion on the possibility of rights issues from existing listed companies, he said.

Asked whether the Reserve Bank's liberalisation of foreign exchange controls would make the exchange more attractive to foreign investors, Barfoot said, "That's not really the issue. More shares need to be listed before they can be bought."
The 57-share industrial index pushed through the key psychological barrier of 10,000 for the first time last month and remains strong, closing Wednesday at 10,031.88 points.
Lower interest rates have made more money available and local investors are propelling prices higher.

The Reserve Bank last week cut its rediscount rate to 23.5 percent from 27 percent, triggering a cut in commercial banks' lending rates. Standard Chartered Bank of Zimbabwe announced on Tuesday it had lowered its lending rate to 25.5 percent from 29.0 percent.
Five new listings scheduled for February, March and April could increase market liquidity by raising the market's capitalisation by more than three percent, Barfoot said.
"For the local investors, who are behind this bull run, these new listings will be very favourably received. Greater liquidity will bring the p/e down," Barfoot said.
The exchange finished 1996 with a market capitalisation of Z$52 billion ($4.7 billion). It now stands at roughly Z$56 billion.

The new listings include Trans Zimbabwe Industries, farming conglomerate CFI Holdings, variable loan company Centennial Property Holdings, plastics manufacturer Randals Holdings and a merchant bank, Barfoot said.
Zimbabwe has enjoyed very good rains and is set for a strong agricultural season, with a positive effect on the stock market.
"The vast majority of people are employed in agriculture. If they have more money to spend this equals a positive situation for the rest fo the country," Barfoot said.
Profits in agriculture-related companies were also likely to be higher because of better crops, he added. ($=Z$11.03) -- Harare newsroom +263-4 72 52 28/9
